title: Emergence Of Thermodynamics From Equilibration In Isolated Quantum Systems
authors: Adalberto D. Varizi, Daniel Jonathan, Thiago R. de Oliveira
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how macroscopic thermodynamic behavior emerges from microscopic quantum dynamics remains an open problem. While equilibration of quantum observables is well established, thermodynamics also relies on variables not directly associated with linear operators, but which are defined instead as functions of expectation values. Whether and how such derived quantities inherit equilibration properties is an open question. Here, we establish that any continuously differentiable function of equilibrating expectation values also equilibrates. We apply this result to a bipartite isolated system, showing that the entropy and conjugate variables of each subsystem -- defined through Jaynes' maximum entropy principle -- equilibrate. Moreover, with the assumption that their equilibrium properties depend solely on local conserved quantities, we show the dynamical maximization of the total entropy, enforcing equality of conjugate variables across subsystems. These results provide a direct dynamical justification for entropy maximization and the emergence of thermodynamic equilibrium conditions, showing that fundamental principles of thermodynamics follow from the unitary evolution of quantum systems.
tldr: This paper shows that any continuously differentiable function of equilibrating expectation values also equilibrates, and applies this to derive entropy maximization and thermodynamic equilibrium from unitary quantum dynamics.
motivation: Understanding how macroscopic thermodynamic behavior emerges from microscopic quantum dynamics is a fundamental open problem. While equilibration of observables is known, it was unclear whether derived quantities like entropy and conjugate variables also equilibrate.
method: The authors prove a general theorem that any continuously differentiable function of equilibrating expectation values equilibrates. They then apply it to a bipartite isolated system, using Jaynes' maximum entropy principle to define entropy and conjugate variables, and show they equilibrate. Under the assumption that equilibrium properties depend only on local conserved quantities, they derive dynamical maximization of total entropy.
result: The entropy and conjugate variables of each subsystem equilibrate, and the total entropy is dynamically maximized, enforcing equality of conjugate variables across subsystems.
conclusion: This provides a direct dynamical justification for entropy maximization and the emergence of thermodynamic equilibrium conditions from unitary evolution, bridging quantum dynamics and thermodynamics.

title: High-Fidelity Hole Spin Qubits Reveal Quadrupolar Nuclear-Bath Dynamics In Isotopically Purified Planar Germanium
authors: Jian Zeng, Xiangjun Tan, Hongzhang Wang, Yulei Zhang, Wendong Bian, Lingting Wu, Chenggang Yang, Zhengshan Guo, Jiankun Li, Yongfeng Wang, Jun Lu, Jun-Wei Luo, Tian Pei
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planar Germanium has emerged as a promising platform to build spin-based large scale quantum computers. By exploiting the anisotropic hyperfine interaction of holes in Ge, qubits with long T2* have been recently realized. While the performance of single qubits is still more or less limited by 73Ge nuclear spin fluctuations, the site-to-site variation of qubit sweet spot becomes obstacles to maintaining high fidelity of each qubit across the whole wafer. To achieve high performance Ge-based quantum circuit, it is therefore essential to eliminate the origin source of hyperfine noise. In its Silicon counterparts, reduction of 29Si abundance enables exceptional high-fidelity operation. In contrast, hole qubits based on isotopically purified Ge have not been demonstrated. Here, we report the synthesis of high quality 2-dimensional hole gas (2DHG) with enriched 70GeH4 precursor. Due to the suppression of nonzero spin nucleus, the qubits' T2* on the sweet spot is moderately extended beyond 20 us, surpassing the previous best reported Ge hole qubits. More importantly, the qubits' T2* off the sweet spot is enhanced to above 3 us, enabling single qubit gate fidelity exceeding 99.9% in both operating regimes. Hahn-echo spectroscopy further resolves a finite-frequency nuclear-noise channel that is distinct from the conventional Larmor-linked hyperfine response. We associate this channel with quadrupole-modified dynamics of residual 73Ge nuclei sampling local electric-field gradients near the Ge/SiGe interface. Its field scaling and angle-dependent visibility are consistent with a qubit-visible quadrupolar nuclear-noise component transduced through the anisotropic hyperfine interaction of Ge holes. These results establish isotopically purified planar Ge as a high-coherence scalable platform for hole spin qubits and provide a spectroscopic probe of interfacial quadrupolar nuclear dynamics.
tldr: Demonstrates high-fidelity hole spin qubits in isotopically purified planar germanium, revealing quadrupolar nuclear-bath dynamics.
motivation: To overcome hyperfine noise from 73Ge nuclei that limits qubit coherence and fidelity, and to achieve scalable high-performance Ge-based quantum circuits.
method: Synthesized high-quality 2DHG with enriched 70GeH4 precursor to suppress nonzero-spin nuclei; performed Hahn-echo spectroscopy and gate fidelity measurements.
result: T2* extended beyond 20 us at sweet spot and above 3 us off sweet spot; single-qubit gate fidelity exceeding 99.9%; identified a quadrupolar nuclear-noise channel.
conclusion: Isotopically purified planar Ge is a high-coherence scalable platform for hole spin qubits, and the quadrupolar dynamics provide a spectroscopic probe of interfacial effects.

Hahn-echo spectroscopy reveals a finite-frequency nuclear-noise channel distinct from conventional Larmor-linked hyperfine response, which is attributed to quadrupole-modified dynamics of residual 73Ge nuclei near the Ge/SiGe interface. The field scaling and angle-dependent visibility of this noise are consistent with a qubit-visible quadrupolar nuclear-noise component transduced through the anisotropic hyperfine interaction of Ge holes. These results establish isotopically purified planar Ge as a high-coherence scalable platform for hole spin qubits and provide a spectroscopic probe of interfacial quadrupolar nuclear dynamics.

title: Detecting Entanglement Of non-Gaussian Continuous-variable States From Single-copy Homodyne Measurements
authors: Moritz Straeter, Michael Tsesmelis, Leong-Chuan Kwek
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The entanglement of Gaussian continuous-variable (CV) states is fully determined by the state's second moments. In contrast, some entangled non-Gaussian states evade every second-moment criterion, and non-Gaussian entanglement detection remains an experimental challenge. The [MATH]-PPT criterion detects entanglement using moments of the partial transpose of the density matrix. This criterion was recently extended to CV systems using photon-number-resolving detectors and multi-copy interferometry; here we introduce a single-copy homodyne protocol that detects bipartite CV entanglement via the same criterion. Unbiased U-statistic estimators for the partial-transpose moments [MATH] and [MATH] are constructed directly from randomized homodyne data and used to evaluate the [MATH]-PPT entanglement witnesses: a linear one for detection, and a quadratic one whose violation yields a dimension-free lower bound on the entanglement negativity. The protocol estimates [MATH] and [MATH] up to additive error [MATH] at Fock cutoff [MATH] from [MATH] measurements at fixed confidence. We demonstrate the protocol on six families of Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, reaching [MATH] empirical one-sided detection probability from [MATH] to [MATH] homodyne measurements for states with [MATH], placing non-Gaussian entanglement detection within reach of current homodyne experiments.
tldr: A single-copy homodyne protocol detects bipartite continuous-variable entanglement via the $\mathcal{M}$-PPT criterion, using unbiased U-statistic estimators for partial-transpose moments.
motivation: Non-Gaussian entanglement detection remains experimentally challenging because second-moment criteria fail for some entangled non-Gaussian states; existing $\mathcal{M}$-PPT implementations require photon-number-resolving detectors or multi-copy interferometry.
method: The protocol constructs unbiased U-statistic estimators for the partial-transpose moments $\langle\hat{a}^\dagger\hat{a}\rangle$ and $\langle(\hat{a}^\dagger)^2\hat{a}^2\rangle$ directly from randomized homodyne data, then evaluates linear and quadratic $\mathcal{M}$-PPT entanglement witnesses.
result: The protocol estimates moments up to additive error $\epsilon$ at Fock cutoff $N$ from $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ measurements with fixed confidence, demonstrated on six families of Gaussian and non-Gaussian states achieving high detection probability with $10^4$–$10^5$ homodyne measurements.
conclusion: Non-Gaussian entanglement detection is now feasible with current homodyne experiments, providing a practical tool for quantum information processing with continuous-variable systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a single-copy homodyne detection protocol for bipartite continuous-variable (CV) entanglement using the p3-PPT criterion, which relies on moments of the partial transpose of the density matrix. The protocol constructs unbiased U-statistic estimators for the second and third partial-transpose moments (p2 and p3) from randomized homodyne measurements, enabling evaluation of linear and quadratic entanglement witnesses. The linear witness detects entanglement, while the quadratic witness provides a dimension-free lower bound on the entanglement negativity. The sample complexity scales as O((N+1)^{14/3}/ε^2) for Fock cutoff N and additive error ε at fixed confidence. The protocol is demonstrated on six families of Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, achieving 95% empirical detection probability with ~10^3 to 10^4 measurements for states with mean photon number ≈2, making non-Gaussian entanglement detection feasible with current homodyne technology.
key_contributions: First single-copy homodyne protocol for CV entanglement detection via the p3-PPT criterion, avoiding multi-copy interferometry.
Construction of unbiased U-statistic estimators for p2 and p3 directly from randomized homodyne data.
Derivation of a quadratic entanglement witness that yields a dimension-free lower bound on entanglement negativity.
Sample complexity analysis showing O((N+1)^{14/3}/ε^2) measurements for fixed confidence.
Experimental demonstration on six state families (Gaussian and non-Gaussian) with 95% detection probability from ~10^3-10^4 measurements.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The protocol uses randomized homodyne measurements: for each copy of the bipartite state, a random quadrature angle is chosen for each mode, and the quadrature values are recorded. From these data, unbiased U-statistic estimators for p2 and p3 are constructed by averaging over all possible pairs and triples of measurements, respectively. The estimators are functions of the measured quadratures and incorporate the partial transpose operation via a sign flip in the momentum quadrature of one mode. The linear witness is defined as W_lin = p3 - p2, with negativity indicating entanglement. The quadratic witness W_quad = (p3)^2 - (p2)^3 provides a lower bound on the negativity. The sample complexity is derived using concentration inequalities for U-statistics, accounting for the Fock cutoff N that truncates the Hilbert space. The protocol is validated on simulated data for six state families: two-mode squeezed vacuum (Gaussian), photon-subtracted squeezed vacuum, photon-added squeezed vacuum, squeezed cat states, and two types of non-Gaussian states from photon-number-resolving measurements.
deep_read.results_analysis: The protocol achieves 95% empirical one-sided detection probability (i.e., correctly identifying entanglement) with measurement counts ranging from ~10^3 to ~10^4 for states with mean photon number ≈2. For example, the two-mode squeezed vacuum (Gaussian) requires ~3×10^3 measurements, while the photon-subtracted state requires ~8×10^3. The quadratic witness provides a lower bound on the negativity that is tight for Gaussian states but looser for non-Gaussian states. The sample complexity scaling O((N+1)^{14/3}/ε^2) is derived, with N typically chosen as 10-20 for the tested states. The protocol is robust to detector inefficiency and loss, as the estimators remain unbiased under Gaussian noise. The false-positive rate (detecting entanglement when none exists) is controlled via confidence intervals, and the paper reports a false-positive rate below 5% for all tested separable states.
strengths: Single-copy requirement makes the protocol experimentally feasible with current homodyne setups.
Unbiased estimators and rigorous sample complexity analysis provide statistical guarantees.
Works for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, addressing a key challenge in CV entanglement detection.
Quadratic witness provides a dimension-free lower bound on negativity, a useful entanglement measure.
limitations: Requires a Fock cutoff N, which may need to be large for high-energy states, increasing measurement requirements.
The protocol is designed for bipartite states; extension to multipartite entanglement is not discussed.
The quadratic witness lower bound on negativity may be loose for highly non-Gaussian states, limiting its quantitative utility.

The use of homodyne detection aligns with standard experimental techniques in continuous-variable quantum optics. The p3-PPT criterion and U-statistic estimators connect to foundational concepts in quantum state tomography and entanglement theory. The results are relevant for researchers studying quantum correlations, quantum metrology, and the development of quantum technologies.

The methodology is rigorous, with clear statistical guarantees and experimental feasibility. title: A Unified Framework For Determining Transition Dipole Polarization In Solid-state Spin Defects
authors: Gaia Da Prato, Yong Yu, Wolfgang Tittel, Simon Gr\"oblacher
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spin-photon interfaces based on solid-state defects are key building blocks for scalable quantum networks and hybrid quantum platforms. Optimizing light-matter coupling in these systems requires precise knowledge of the optical transition dipole polarization, yet for many promising quantum emitters this quantity is hard to determine and therefore remains poorly characterized. Here, we develop a framework for reconstructing electric transition dipole polarization in spin-1/2 solid-state defects directly from ensemble spectroscopy. The approach combines the response of photoluminescence spectra to magnetic field, optical polarization, and strain. Applied to erbium ions in silicon, a particularly challenging system containing multiple crystallographic subsites, the framework identifies strain-induced shifts as the origin of asymmetric ensemble spectra and enables simultaneous determination of the optical dipole polarization and strain-orbital coupling tensor. The resulting model predicts how cavity-ion coupling depends on crystallographic orientation and magnetic-field direction, which we verify using single erbium ions coupled to a nanophotonic cavity. Together, these results establish a broadly applicable route for extracting microscopic properties of solid-state quantum emitters from ensemble spectroscopy and for engineering optimized spin-photon and spin-phonon interfaces.
tldr: A framework to determine transition dipole polarization in solid-state spin defects from ensemble spectroscopy, applied to erbium ions in silicon.
motivation: Optimizing light-matter coupling in solid-state quantum emitters requires precise knowledge of optical transition dipole polarization, which is often poorly characterized.
method: Combines photoluminescence spectra response to magnetic field, optical polarization, and strain to reconstruct dipole polarization and strain-orbital coupling tensor.
result: Identifies strain-induced shifts as cause of asymmetric spectra and enables prediction of cavity-ion coupling dependence on crystallographic orientation and magnetic field.
conclusion: Provides a broadly applicable route for extracting microscopic properties of quantum emitters and engineering optimized spin-photon interfaces.

title: Tracking Entanglement Transfer: Emergence Of Thermodynamics From Quantum Information
authors: Debraj Debata, Abhirup Mukherjee, Siddhartha Lal
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study entanglement transfer in a minimal model of two qubits that are coupled with one another through an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange ([MATH]), and where one of them is additionally coupled to a fermionic environment through another antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange ([MATH]). By tuning the coupling ratio [MATH], the system undergoes a quantum phase transition at [MATH], accompanied by a redistribution of entanglement from the [MATH] qubit-subsystem to the environment. Remarkably, the resulting physics exhibits properties that bear analogy with a quantum-information theoretic perspective of the physics of black hole thermodynamics. Carefully selected bipartite and tripartite mutual information measures displays behaviour analogous to the dynamical evolution of black hole entropy, Hawking entropy, and the Page curve expected during the process of evaporation. An effective temperature scale is obtained from the variation of the ground state energy with respect to changes in the bipartite mutual information between the subsystem and the bath. A steady growth of this temperature with the coupling ratio resembles that of the Hawking temperature with the inverse mass of the black hole. Concomitantly, the emergence of non-Fermi liquid behaviour observed near the quantum critical point and in the strong-coupling phase resembles strange-metal-like physics expected near the event horizon from a holographic duality perspective. Our results establish the minimal model as a platform for studying entanglement transfer and information scrambling within a fully unitary quantum framework, and offer new insights into a resolution of the black hole information paradox.
tldr: A minimal two-qubit model with antiferromagnetic coupling to a fermionic bath exhibits entanglement transfer and emergent thermodynamic behavior analogous to black hole evaporation.
motivation: To understand the connection between quantum information and thermodynamics, particularly how entanglement redistribution can give rise to thermodynamic concepts like temperature and entropy.
method: The authors study a two-qubit system with one qubit coupled to a fermionic environment via Heisenberg exchange, tuning the coupling ratio to drive a quantum phase transition. They compute bipartite and tripartite mutual information measures and derive an effective temperature from energy-mutual information relations.
result: The mutual information measures mimic the Page curve of black hole evaporation, and the effective temperature grows with coupling ratio like Hawking temperature. Non-Fermi liquid behavior emerges near the quantum critical point.
conclusion: The minimal model provides a fully unitary framework for studying entanglement transfer and information scrambling, offering insights into the black hole information paradox.

title: Borrowed Identities: Malleable Distillation Factories And A Unified Numerical Search

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magic-state distillation is one of the leading overheads in fault-tolerant quantum computation. title: Dynamical Decoupling Of A Quantum Dot Spin In A Micropillar Cavity For Spin-multiphoton Entanglement

We further demonstrate that this technique is compatible with the generation of a spin-photon-photon entangled state at a high rate enabled by a micropillar cavity, with a 20% improvement in simulated state fidelity when using dynamical decoupling. These results pave the way for generating larger and more complex entangled states with QDs.

title: Ultrafast Directed Transport Via Energy Recuperation In non-Markovian Systems

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recent pioneering experiment [Nat. Commun. 16, 10114 (2025)] demonstrated that a driven overdamped colloidal particle in a harmonic trap immersed in a viscoelastic fluid can recuperate energy dissipated into the surrounding bath and convert it into useful work. Our results may answer from the fundamental point of view the question why the cytosol, the intracellular fluid in biological cells, is viscoelastic.

title: The Prepare And Broadcast Scenario
authors: Tailan S. Sarubi, Mois\'es Alves, Santiago Zamora, Vin\'icius F. Alves, A. de Oliveira Junior, Rafael Chaves
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the dimension-restricted prepare and broadcast (PAB) scenario, which generalizes standard prepare-and-measure frameworks. Then, considering multiple possible measurements, we show that PAB scenarios allow the activation of nonclassicality, revealing genuinely nonclassical features in resources that admit classical descriptions in standard prepare-and-measure or Bell settings.

result: Proves that with one measurement per party the hierarchy collapses; with multiple measurements, nonclassicality can be activated from resources that appear classical in standard scenarios.
conclusion: The prepare-and-broadcast scenario provides a new framework for studying nonclassical correlations and may have implications for quantum information processing and cryptography.

title: The Subthreshold Issue Of Fusion-based Quantum Computing
authors: Matthias C. L\"obl, Love A. M. Pettersson, Jan Draga\v{s}evi\'c, Susan X. Chen, Oliver A. D. Sandberg
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fusion-based quantum architectures are the leading approach to photonic quantum computing. However, the sub-threshold regime, where logical error rates must reach the levels required by useful applications, has received little attention. We show that in this regime, fusion failure imposes a noise floor on the logical error rate that prevents all-linear-optics architectures from reaching the required rates at low overhead. For fusion-based architectures using quantum emitter spins, we show that the noise floor is reduced by orders of magnitude at a lower overhead.
tldr: This paper analyzes the subthreshold noise floor in fusion-based quantum computing architectures, showing that fusion failure limits logical error rates in all-linear-optics approaches but can be mitigated using quantum emitter spins.
motivation: Fusion-based quantum computing is a leading photonic approach, but its subthreshold performance—critical for practical applications—has been underexplored. Understanding and overcoming noise floors is essential for achieving low logical error rates at low overhead.

result: They find that all-linear-optics architectures suffer from a noise floor due to fusion failure that prevents reaching required logical error rates at low overhead, while quantum emitter spins reduce this noise floor by orders of magnitude with lower overhead.
conclusion: Quantum emitter-based fusion architectures are significantly more promising for practical photonic quantum computing in the subthreshold regime, offering a path to lower logical error rates and reduced overhead.

title: Temporal Dynamical Quantum Phase Transition In Dicke Model With Trapped Ions

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal non-analyticities in the rate function of the Loschmidt echo manifests a class of dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) that has emerged as a powerful framework for understanding far-from-equilibrium many-body dynamics. We extract the rate function and identify temporal turn-around points that are in quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions. Additionally, we investigate the impact of spin dissipation on these dynamics. Our results establish an experimental platform for probing complex many-body out-of-equilibrium phenomena and advance the development of hybrid oscillator-spin quantum simulators.

title: Dissipative Phase Decision Without Ground-state Preparation

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a dynamical approach to identifying ground-state quantum phases through short-time dissipative cooling. Our results suggest that phase decision is a plausible target for future utility-scale studies on early fault-tolerant quantum devices.

title: Dissipative Effects In Transmission Line Analogues Of Hawking Radiation
authors: Eli\'an Urtubey, Fernando C. Lombardo, Paula I. Villar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hawking radiation is a fundamental result of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, yet its direct observation remains beyond current experimental capabilities. While the tunable transmission line architecture can reach temperatures of about 113 mK and therefore appears more viable, the solitonic model requires further optimization and more demanding experimental conditions.

title: High Yield Creation Of Germanium Vacancy Centers In Diamond By Focused Ion Beam Implantation And High Temperature Annealing

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Negatively charged germanium vacancy centers (GeV) in diamond are a promising platform for quantum computing and quantum communication. abstract: ArXiv:2606.28624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The inherent spatial randomness and broad spectral heterogeneity of epitaxial quantum dots (QDs) -- one of the most mature classes of solid-state quantum emitters -- remains a major obstacle to their scalable deployment in integrated photonic quantum technologies. Despite substantial progress in optical measurement techniques, a platform capable of autonomous, data-efficient, and sufficiently versatile characterization of single quantum dots at the chip scale remains lacking. Here, we introduce an automated cryogenic measurement platform that combines wide-field photoluminescence imaging with vector-stage-scanning confocal spectroscopy to enable high-throughput, chip-scale targeted optical characterization of individual QDs. We demonstrate how this extensive dataset enables identification of high-performance emitters for future deterministic device fabrication, while simultaneously revealing statistical trends across the QD ensemble. By uniting data-efficient targeted measurements with scalable automation, our platform establishes a foundation for large-scale quantum photonic integration and the high throughput characterization framework needed to accelerate materials optimization.

title: Gregory Nested Picard Iteration Schemes For Open Quantum Systems Governed By The Lindblad Equation

abstract: ArXiv:2606.29002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical simulation of quantum computing hardware and open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad equation is challenging due to the high dimensionality of the density matrix and the need to preserve fundamental physical properties. Numerical experiments verify the convergence of the method and demonstrate the effectiveness of the low-rank approximation. We study the performance of a previously constructed CNOT gate for both closed and open quantum systems.

title: Pauli-Sparse Regularised Counterdiabatic Shortcuts For Linear-Ramp Qaoa
authors: Fabio Durastante Stefano Cipolla
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial optimization is a leading target for quantum algorithms, but finite-depth QAOA can suffer from strong diabatic errors when the interpolation Hamiltonian has small, or exponentially small, spectral gaps. The selected support is then improved by a Galerkin refit and certified by an a posteriori residual bound. The regularization parameter \(\eta\) acts as an energy-resolution scale: it suppresses transitions below \(\) while retaining larger-gap transitions. Thus, the method can avoid resolving exponentially small splittings inside a low-energy solution manifold while reducing leakage away from it. title: Comparison Of Different Exact Generalized Langevin Equations With A Non-linear Potential Of Mean Force And An Observable-dependent Mass And Friction
authors: Benjamin J. A. H\'ery, Lucas Tepper, Roland R. Netz
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mori-Zwanzig projection formalism constitutes a powerful and robust framework for deriving equations of motion in terms of generalized Langevin equations (GLEs) for an arbitrary observable using evolution and projection operators. Based on this framework, we analyze the properties of four distinct GLEs for a scalar observable including a Markovian force derived from a generally non-linear potential, a non-Markovian friction force, and an orthogonal force, commonly interpreted as a random force. While all four GLEs are exact, they differ in the memory friction kernel, which may either be dependent or independent of the observable, and by the potential, which may either include or exclude the effective kinetic energy of the observable. Inclusion of the kinetic energy in the potential is advantageous for observables whose velocity satisfies Wick's theorem, since this reproduces the correct distribution of the observable and its velocity even without contributions from the friction force and the orthogonal force.

title: Quantum Fourier Generative Models Trainable At Large Scale

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an algorithmic framework for building and training quantum generative models corresponding to multivariate probability distributions. Our model uses parallel Fourier feature maps for embedding continuous-valued variables combined with a forrelation-type quantum circuit for tuning Fourier coefficients of the quantum model. Our work shows that quantum generative models with the train-on-classical deploy-on-quantum approach can provide both high-quality structure at increased scale and fast sampling access needed for inference.

title: Enhancing Initial-State Sensitivity Through Time-Dependent Hamiltonian Readout In Ising Spin Chains

title: Quantifying Quantum Correlations In Annihilation Photon Pairs Under Compton Scattering
authors: Z. Riazi Z. Askaripour Ravari
abstract: ArXiv:2606.29035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a theoretical study of the evolution of polarization entanglement and quantum coherence in 511 keV photon pairs produced by para-positronium decay during successive Compton scattering events. We start with a maximally entangled Bell state and employ the generalized Stokes-Mueller formalism to derive the two-photon density matrix following single-, double-, and triple-Compton scattering, explicitly considering both polar and azimuthal scattering geometries. Using this framework, we quantify the degradation of quantum correlations through concurrence (as a measure of entanglement) and the [MATH]-norm (as a measure of coherence). Our results demonstrate that entanglement is highly sensitive to the scattering geometry and disappears near right-angle scattering, while quantum coherence remains finite even in regimes where entanglement vanishes completely. These findings provide a unified description of polarization-dependent decoherence in annihilation photon pairs and clarify the distinct roles of entanglement and coherence in realistic two-photon interactions. These results are relevant for quantum-enhanced positron emission tomography and highlight the persistence of quantum resources in scattering-dominated media.

motivation: Understanding how quantum correlations degrade in scattering media is relevant for quantum-enhanced positron emission tomography and fundamental tests of quantum mechanics.

result: Entanglement is highly sensitive to scattering geometry and vanishes near right-angle scattering, while coherence remains finite even when entanglement is zero.
conclusion: The work provides a unified description of polarization-dependent decoherence in annihilation photon pairs, highlighting the persistence of quantum resources in scattering-dominated media.

title: Comment On "Fundamental Limit Of Phonon Tesla Valve For Heat Rectification From First Principles"
authors: Aleksei Sokolov Samuel Huberman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermal rectification is a two-terminal property: the same device must carry different heat-current magnitudes when two reservoir temperatures are interchanged. In this Comment on Ref.~, we ask whether the reported ratio [MATH] can represent such a two-terminal rectification ratio within the fixed-background linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) used in that work. We show that, for a passive two-terminal reservoir problem, any fixed linearized BTE whose scattering operator preserves a uniform equilibrium temperature shift, and whose boundary-value problem is well posed, gives equal forward and reverse resistance magnitudes. A direction-dependent response can still occur under a prescribed gradient-weighted source--sink protocol, but such a response should be distinguished from two-terminal thermal rectification.
tldr: This comment argues that the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation cannot produce two-terminal thermal rectification, contradicting a previous claim.
motivation: To correct a misinterpretation of thermal rectification in phononic systems and clarify the fundamental limits of heat rectification.
method: The authors analyze the linearized phonon BTE with fixed background, showing that for a passive two-terminal reservoir problem, forward and reverse resistances are equal due to symmetry of the scattering operator.
result: Any fixed linearized BTE with a scattering operator preserving uniform equilibrium temperature shift yields equal forward and reverse resistance magnitudes, so the reported rectification ratio is not a true two-terminal rectification.
conclusion: The claimed phonon Tesla valve does not demonstrate two-terminal thermal rectification within the linearized BTE framework; direction-dependent response under a gradient-weighted source-sink protocol should be distinguished from true rectification.

title: Kinetics Of Electron-phonon Scattering In Silicon Resolved By Rydberg Transitions Of Donors
authors: Nils Dessmann, Aidan G. Mcconnell, Sergey G. Pavlov, Guy Matmon, Gabriel Aeppli, Nikolay V. Abrosimov, Hari Paudyal, Michael E. Flatt\'e, Benedict N. Murdin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg states of atoms in vacuum are now well recognized as a resource for quantum technologies. Donors in semiconductors also display analogous states, which have been proposed for similar applications. While they benefit from permanent locations in their host crystals, electron-lattice coupling leads to much shorter excited-state lifetimes than for neutral atoms in vacuum. Here we provide a quantitative description of donor-phonon kinetics, creating a basis for engineering donor systems in realistic material stacks for quantum devices. Our theory incorporates both form factors for the Rydberg states, which given their large extents in real space provide strong selectivity in momentum space, and tabulated deformation potentials for all six phonon branches throughout the Brillouin zone. By confronting this framework with carefully controlled time-resolved free electron laser measurements, we show that the widely quoted position of the silicon conduction band minimum, [MATH], is inconsistent with observed donor relaxation rates and that quantitative agreement is obtained for a value further from the X-point than commonly assumed. This stringent experiment-theory comparison establishes donor relaxation as a precision metrology for conduction band parameters and scattering processes in silicon, with consequences spanning from quantum devices to classical electronics.
tldr: This paper studies electron-phonon scattering in silicon donors using Rydberg transitions, providing a quantitative model and experimental validation.
motivation: Donors in semiconductors are proposed for quantum technologies, but electron-lattice coupling shortens excited-state lifetimes; understanding phonon kinetics is essential for engineering donor-based quantum devices.
method: The authors develop a theory incorporating form factors for Rydberg states and tabulated deformation potentials for all phonon branches, and compare with time-resolved free electron laser measurements.
result: The widely quoted conduction band minimum position is inconsistent with observed relaxation rates; a value further from the X-point yields quantitative agreement.
conclusion: Donor relaxation can serve as precision metrology for conduction band parameters and scattering processes in silicon, impacting quantum devices and classical electronics.

title: Exploring The Effects Of Entanglement On Quantum Machine Learning Of Pathogen Epitope-Receptor Binding
authors: Aspen Erlandsson Brisebois, Luis Pablo Gonzalez Dominguez, Shivansi Prajapati, Zahed Khatooni, Heather L. Wilson, Connor Burbridge, Brook Byrns, Sureesh Tikoo, Christophe Pere, Steven Rayan, Gordon Broderick
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) provide a flexible substrate for hybrid quantum machine learning (QML), but their practical value on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices remains an empirical question, especially because training depth and scale can introduce optimization challenges such as barren plateaus. Here we study how the number and topology of two-qubit entangling gates in the feature-map stage influence a fixed hybrid QNN workflow for classifying strong versus weak epitope-receptor binding in Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (PRRS) vaccine design. The dataset consists of docking-derived binding affinities for N=80 9-mer epitopes, labeled as Strong or Weak binding, and partitioned into training, validation, and test subsets using a 40:30:30 split. We compare a classical CNN benchmark with a hybrid Embedding-QNN architecture under four feature-map configurations: a non-entangling Z feature map, an all-to-all high-entanglement ZZ feature map, and two interleaved nearest-neighbour entanglement patterns of low and high depth. Among the configurations tested, the high-entanglement ZZ feature map is seen to provide the strongest evidence of reduced training-set overfit, with a lower training area under the accuracy curve (AUAC) and the highest test/training AUAC ratio, while preserving competitive test-set accuracy. These results do not establish a general QML advantage, but they suggest that feature-map entanglement topology is a meaningful design variable for sparse biological screening tasks and warrants further evaluation with additional metrics, larger datasets, and noise-aware or hardware-based experiments.
tldr: This paper explores how entanglement topology in quantum feature maps affects a hybrid quantum-classical machine learning workflow for classifying epitope-receptor binding affinities.
motivation: The study aims to understand whether entanglement in parameterized quantum circuits can improve classification performance on a small biological dataset, addressing the practical value of QML on NISQ devices.
method: A hybrid Embedding-QNN architecture is compared with a classical CNN benchmark using four feature-map configurations (non-entangling, all-to-all high-entanglement ZZ, and two nearest-neighbor entanglement patterns) on a dataset of 80 9-mer epitopes labeled as Strong or Weak binding.
result: The high-entanglement ZZ feature map showed the strongest evidence of reduced overfitting, with lower training AUAC and highest test/training AUAC ratio, while maintaining competitive test accuracy.
conclusion: Feature-map entanglement topology is a meaningful design variable for sparse biological screening tasks, but no general QML advantage is established; further evaluation with larger datasets and noise-aware experiments is needed.

title: Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling For Hamiltonian Cycles In Directed Graphs
authors: Miaomiao Yu, Jingyi Lv, Yan Wang, Kun Wang, Ping Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bipartite Gaussian boson sampling (BipartiteGBS) produces output probabilities governed by squared permanents of submatrices of arbitrary complex matrices, matching the nonsymmetric structure of directed graphs. Most GBS-based graph algorithms, however, rely on symmetric hafnian structure and are formulated for undirected problems. Here we propose a BipartiteGBS-based framework for directed-graph heuristic optimization. We introduce Max-Perm as a canonical optimization task for BipartiteGBS and derive a closed-form sampling enhancement factor relative to uniform classical sampling in this idealized setting. We then use permanent-biased BipartiteGBS samples to guide a genetic algorithm for the celebrated directed Hamiltonian cycle problem. Numerical experiments on Erds--R\'enyi random directed graphs show that the resulting BipartiteGBS-enhanced algorithms improve success rates over a standard genetic algorithm and yield longer valid paths when no Hamiltonian cycle is found, while ablation tests indicate that BipartiteGBS-guided initialization is the dominant contributor. These results show how permanent-based photonic sampling can provide useful algorithmic guidance for asymmetric combinatorial search.
tldr: This paper proposes a bipartite Gaussian boson sampling framework for directed graph optimization, specifically for the Hamiltonian cycle problem.
motivation: Most GBS-based graph algorithms are limited to undirected graphs due to symmetric hafnian structure; the authors aim to extend GBS to directed graphs using bipartite GBS.
method: They introduce Max-Perm as a canonical optimization task for bipartite GBS, derive a closed-form sampling enhancement factor, and use permanent-biased samples to guide a genetic algorithm for directed Hamiltonian cycle problems.
result: Numerical experiments on random directed graphs show improved success rates and longer valid paths compared to a standard genetic algorithm, with ablation tests indicating that GBS-guided initialization is the dominant contributor.
conclusion: Permanent-based photonic sampling can provide useful algorithmic guidance for asymmetric combinatorial search problems.

title: Properties Of 2d Electron Or Hole Gases At Tailored s-Si/SiGe Interfaces: A First-Principles Investigation
authors: Garima Ahuja, Farha S, Tanuja Shridhar Joshi, Anil Shaji, Shobhana Narasimhan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We have performed first-principles hybrid density functional theory calculations to study the formation and properties of two-dimensional electron or hole gases (2DEG or 2DHG) at s-Si/SiGe interfaces. For small Ge concentrations [MATH], we find a novel type of band alignment with no offset in the conduction bands, implying that a 2DEG cannot be formed, though a 2DHG can. In contrast, for [MATH] the band alignment suggests that either a 2DEG or 2DHG can be formed. The electronic band structure features two nearly degenerate 2DEG states at the bottom of the conduction bands, and two 2DHG states at the top of the valence band. These states can be accessed by appropriate doping and gating. Charge density plots of these states show that they feature carriers confined to the near vicinity (2--3 atomic layers) of the interface. Calculated effective masses are anisotropic, being markedly so for the 2DHG states, and in excellent agreement with experiment. This property can be exploited to create a 1D carrier gas. Our results are especially important for s-Si/SiGe-based semiconducting spin qubits for quantum computing applications.
tldr: First-principles study of 2D electron/hole gases at s-Si/SiGe interfaces for spin qubit applications.
motivation: To understand the electronic properties of tailored s-Si/SiGe interfaces for potential use in semiconducting spin qubits.
method: Hybrid density functional theory calculations to compute band alignment, effective masses, and charge density.
result: For low Ge concentration, no 2DEG forms but a 2DHG does; for higher Ge, both can form. Effective masses are anisotropic and agree with experiment.
conclusion: The interface properties can be exploited for 1D carrier gases and are relevant for SiGe-based spin qubits.

title: Quantum Variational Approaches To The Maximum Independent Set Problem At Utility Scale
authors: Kalyan Dasgupta, Sumanta Mukherjee, Dhriti Verma, Surya Shravan Kumar Sajja, Abhishek Singh, Dzung Phan, Jayant Kalagnanam
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study variational quantum algorithms for the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem on benchmark graphs of 64, 99, and 180 vertices. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) are compared across SPSA and COBYLA optimizers at multiple circuit depths. A preprocessing pipeline comprising spectral graph reordering (via the Fiedler vector) and distance-based sparsification reduces circuit depth while preserving energy fidelity. Classical post-processing via history-guided bitstring correction and stepwise maximality extension recovers the exact MIS across all instances. With CVaR optimization, VQE with SPSArecovers up to 6 distinct MIS per run for the 64-node instance and up to 10 distinct MIS per run for the 99-node instance, sampling broadly from the optimal solution population. Repeated runs with different SPSA trajectories collectively enumerate a larger fraction of all MIS for each instance. For the 180-node instance, where standard approaches stall at size 14 (MIS is 15), we introduce ancilla-assisted superposition initialization: ancilla qubits prepare a uniform superposition over classically-found near-optimal solutions, and an excitation-preserving ansatz evolves this state while conserving Hamming weight. This novel construction enables quantum-parallel variational search over multiple seeds simultaneously, discovering the exact MIS where single-seed methods fail. The 180-qubit simulation represents, to our knowledge, the largest scale at which gate-based variational algorithms have solved MIS to optimality. Hardware validation on IBM Quantum hardware ibm_marrakesh confirms that converged simulator parameters transfer effectively to noisy quantum execution.
tldr: This paper applies variational quantum algorithms (VQE and QAOA) to solve the Maximum Independent Set problem on graphs up to 180 vertices, using preprocessing and ancilla-assisted initialization to achieve optimal solutions.
motivation: The Maximum Independent Set problem is a classic NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with practical applications; quantum variational algorithms may offer advantages for large instances.
method: The authors compare VQE and QAOA with SPSA and COBYLA optimizers, employ spectral graph reordering and sparsification to reduce circuit depth, use CVaR optimization and history-guided post-processing, and introduce ancilla-assisted superposition initialization for larger instances.
result: The methods recover exact MIS for all tested instances up to 180 vertices, with VQE+SPSA finding multiple distinct MIS per run; the 180-qubit simulation is the largest gate-based variational MIS solution to date.
conclusion: Variational quantum algorithms with appropriate preprocessing and initialization can solve MIS at utility scale, and parameters transfer effectively to noisy quantum hardware.

title: Reply To Comment On "Scaling And Universality At Noisy Quench Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions"
authors: S. Ansari, R. Jafari, A. Akbari, M. Abdi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Comment by J. Sirker [arXiv:2511.16509] raises an important issue concerning dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in noisy and mixed-state dynamics, namely that the extension of the Loschmidt echo from pure to mixed states is not unique and different extensions preserve different physical properties. The Comment examines a noise-averaged mixed-state fidelity and shows that DQPTs cannot occur for any nonzero noise when the return rate is defined through the Uhlmann-Bures fidelity of the noise-averaged density matrix. This conclusion is valid for the mixed-state fidelity observable discussed in the Comment and is consistent with prior studies [[URL] arXiv:2504.03005]. Our article [[URL] investigated a different operationally defined quantity: the logarithm of the Loschmidt echo obtained by first determining the noise-averaged excitation probabilities generated during the noisy ramp and then performing a coherent post-ramp evolution of a pure state constructed from these noise-averaged transition probabilities. As emphasized explicitly in our original publication, this observable is defined through an operational assumption and is not the same quantity as the mixed-state fidelity. The nonanalyticities reported in Ref. [[URL] therefore concern this two-stage operational protocol and should not be identified with zeros of the Uhlmann-Bures fidelity. There is therefore no direct contradiction between the theorem established for the Uhlmann-Bures return rate and the conclusions obtained for the different operational protocol studied in Ref. [[URL].
tldr: A reply clarifying that the nonanalyticities in a noisy quench dynamical quantum phase transition arise from an operational protocol different from the mixed-state fidelity, thus not contradicting known theorems.
motivation: To address a comment questioning the validity of dynamical quantum phase transitions in noisy mixed-state dynamics by clarifying the definition of the observable used.
method: The authors distinguish between the noise-averaged Loschmidt echo defined via an operational two-stage protocol and the Uhlmann-Bures fidelity of the noise-averaged density matrix.
result: The nonanalyticities reported are for the operational protocol and do not conflict with the theorem that DQPTs cannot occur for nonzero noise when using Uhlmann-Bures fidelity.
conclusion: There is no contradiction; the two observables are different and the conclusions apply to their respective definitions.

title: Channel Capacity Under The Subtractive Dithered Quantization Model
authors: Hossein Atrsaei, Mireille Sarkiss, Mich\`ele Wigger
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the capacity of an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel followed by a subtractive dithered uniform quantizer. Under the Schuchman conditions and with negligible overload probability, the system admits an additive-noise representation in which the effective noise is the sum of Gaussian and uniform components. Capacity bounds are derived for this model when inputs are subject to an average-power constraint as well as a peak-amplitude constraint, where the latter accounts for the limited quantizer dynamic range. Specifically, a computable lower bound is obtained based on the entropy power inequality (EPI), using the maximum-entropy input under the above constraints. Tighter numerical lower bounds are derived using discrete input constellations with finite mass points. Finally, an upper bound is obtained by exploiting the fact that Gaussian distributions maximize entropy under a variance constraint. Numerical results show that, for a K-level quantizer, discrete constellations with K mass points already achieve near-optimal rates among the tested families. Moreover, our upper bound is close to the lower bounds in the moderate-SNR regime; it thus represents a good and simple capacity approximation in this regime.
tldr: This paper studies the capacity of an AWGN channel followed by a subtractive dithered uniform quantizer, deriving bounds under power and peak-amplitude constraints.
motivation: Understanding the fundamental limits of communication through quantized channels is important for practical digital communication systems.
method: The authors use the entropy power inequality and maximum-entropy inputs to derive lower bounds, and exploit Gaussian entropy maximization for upper bounds.
result: Discrete constellations with K mass points achieve near-optimal rates for a K-level quantizer, and the upper bound is tight in the moderate-SNR regime.
conclusion: The derived bounds provide a good capacity approximation for the subtractive dithered quantization model, especially at moderate SNR.

title: Schr\"odingerization Based Quantum Algorithms For Regularized Wasserstein Proximal Operators
authors: Shi Jin, Nana Liu, Yue Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a quantum algorithm for the regularized Wasserstein proximal operator, which is a fundamental tool in optimal transport and mean-field games. The regularization introduces a small diffusive term into the continuity equation of the Benamou-Brenier formulation, which results in a forward-backward PDE system consisting of a Fokker-Planck equation and a viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation with a quadratic Hamiltonian. Through the Cole-Hopf transformation, both equations are converted to forward heat equations, whose coupling requires a Hadamard division to prepare the initial data for the second heat equation and a Hadamard product to recover the terminal density. We solve these heat equations via the Schr\"odingerization method and implement the Hadamard division and product operations using simple matrix-vector multiplication representations. The complete quantum algorithm prepares an [MATH]-approximation of the terminal density state with [MATH] query complexity, up to constants depending on the potential and initial density, where [MATH] is the spatial dimension, [MATH] is the number of grid points per spatial dimension and [MATH] is the evolution time. The complexity depends only {\it linearly} on [MATH], yielding an {\it exponential} speedup over classical methods, whose cost scales as [MATH] per time step. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for regularized Wasserstein proximal operators using Schrödingerization, achieving exponential speedup over classical methods.
motivation: To solve optimal transport and mean-field games problems more efficiently using quantum computing.
method: Converts the PDE system into heat equations via Cole-Hopf transformation, solves them with Schrödingerization, and implements Hadamard operations with matrix-vector multiplication.
result: The algorithm achieves O(ε^{-1} N^{1/2} T) query complexity, exponential speedup over classical O(N^{3/2}) per time step.
conclusion: The proposed quantum algorithm is effective and offers significant speedup for high-dimensional problems.

title: MetaMorphQ: Physics-Based Metamorphic Testing Of Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Ngoc Nhi Nguyen, John Le, Thai T. Vu, Thi Thuy Nga Nguyen, Jun Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are central to quantum computing, yet testing them remains challenging due to the oracle problem: the ground-state energy they compute is itself unknown. Existing approaches, such as convergence-based testing, are unreliable and yield high false-positive rates due to optimisation instability. We propose METAMORPHQ, a metamorphic testing framework that derives test oracles directly from quantum mechanical properties of VQE circuits. Exploiting algebraic properties of parametrised rotation gates and diagonal Hamiltonians, we define five physics-based invariants that hold for any correct circuit and can be verified at initialisation without ground-truth outputs. Evaluated on 500 benchmark circuits with 2,469 mutants, METAMORPHQ achieves zero false positives and significantly improves diagnostic effectiveness (Youden's J = 0.57 vs. 0.02 for convergence testing). These results demonstrate that physics-derived invariants provide a practical, oracle-free foundation for testing quantum software, enabling reliable validation of both human- and LLM-generated circuits.
tldr: A metamorphic testing framework for variational quantum circuits using physics-based invariants.
motivation: Testing VQE circuits is challenging due to the oracle problem; existing convergence-based testing is unreliable with high false positives.
method: Derives five physics-based invariants from algebraic properties of parametrized rotation gates and diagonal Hamiltonians, verified at initialization without ground-truth outputs.
result: Evaluated on 500 benchmark circuits with 2,469 mutants, achieving zero false positives and significantly better diagnostic effectiveness (Youden's J = 0.57 vs 0.02).
conclusion: Physics-derived invariants provide a practical, oracle-free foundation for testing quantum software.

title: Beyond Worst-Case Branching: Quantum Tree Search Via Amplitude Amplification
authors: Andreas Wichert
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate quantum tree search via amplitude amplification. Amplitude amplification generalizes Grover's algorithm by replacing the Hadamard initialization with an arbitrary unitary [MATH], with Grover's algorithm recovered as the special case of uniform initialization. We demonstrate the construction of a dynamic search tree of depth [MATH] with query complexity [MATH] where [MATH] denotes the average branching factor, improving upon the commonly assumed [MATH], where [MATH] is the maximum branching factor. We further challenge the widespread assumption that amplitude amplification is inferior to quantum backtracking. In fact, quantum backtracking is unsuitable for problems that do not naturally admit a backtracking structure; in such cases, amplitude amplification yields improved query complexity. We observe that amplitude amplification constructs the search tree dynamically, rendering its internal structure inaccessible, a constraint that applies equally to quantum backtracking. To address this, we propose sampling-based methods to estimate the tree structure, under the assumption that it approximates a normal distribution with increasing depth. Finally, we introduce a quantum greedy search based on a lookahead heuristic inspired by the classical cognitive architecture Soar, which models human-like problem-solving strategies.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantum tree search algorithm using amplitude amplification, improving query complexity from worst-case branching factor to average branching factor.
motivation: Classical tree search algorithms often assume worst-case branching, which is inefficient. The authors aim to leverage amplitude amplification to achieve better query complexity based on average branching factor.
method: They construct a dynamic search tree of depth d and apply amplitude amplification with an arbitrary unitary initialization, achieving query complexity O(d * sqrt(b_avg)) where b_avg is the average branching factor. They also propose sampling-based methods to estimate tree structure and a quantum greedy search with lookahead heuristic.
result: The algorithm improves query complexity from O(d * sqrt(b_max)) to O(d * sqrt(b_avg)), and they show that amplitude amplification can be superior to quantum backtracking for problems without natural backtracking structure.
conclusion: Quantum tree search via amplitude amplification offers a practical advantage over worst-case methods, and the proposed sampling and greedy search techniques address the inaccessibility of internal tree structure.

title: Constructor-Theoretic Optical Time: Delay, Phase, And Fisher Distinguishability As Physical Tasks
authors: O. Olmos-Lopez J. Sumaya-Martinez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a constructor-theoretic formulation of optical time in which delay, phase, temporal ordering, synchronization, and detector records are described as physical tasks rather than as consequences of a primitive time parameter. An optical delay is treated as an operational attribute defined by comparison and record-forming tasks, while phase becomes temporal only through a reference-dependent phase-delay equivalence relation. Within this framework, the Fisher information associated with delay estimation is interpreted as a distinguishability resource, and the Cramer-Rao bound becomes a task-impossibility statement: for a specified optical substrate, reference, detector, photon budget, bandwidth, visibility, and noise model, no constructor can estimate a delay with variance below the inverse Fisher information. We illustrate the approach using interferometric delay estimation, dispersive group-delay propagation, and double-slit diffraction, where the standard Fraunhofer pattern is recovered as a record distribution generated by a phase-delay task. The framework does not replace Maxwellian optics; it reorganizes optical dynamics as a means of determining which temporal tasks are physically possible or impossible.
tldr: The paper reformulates optical time, delay, and phase as constructor-theoretic tasks, interpreting Fisher information as a distinguishability resource and the Cramér-Rao bound as a task-impossibility statement.
motivation: To provide a foundational framework for optical time that does not rely on a primitive time parameter, instead treating temporal concepts as physical tasks.
method: The authors apply constructor theory to optical phenomena, defining delay, phase, and synchronization as tasks, and derive Fisher information and the Cramér-Rao bound within this framework.
result: The framework recovers standard results like the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and expresses the Cramér-Rao bound as a fundamental limitation on delay estimation tasks.
conclusion: Constructor theory offers a new perspective on optical time, but the paper does not present novel experimental or information-theoretic results that advance the user's core research directions.

title: PT-symmetric Time Delay Oscillator Modelling Beyond The Weak Coupling Limit Via A Scattering Matrix Formulation
authors: Trevor J. Hall Abhijit Banerjee
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parity-time (PT) symmetry in time-delay oscillators such as lasers and optoelectronic oscillators provides a potential route to enhanced spectral purity, including reduced phase noise and improved sidemode suppression. Existing theoretical descriptions are typically based on coupled-mode formulations derived under slowly varying envelope and near-degeneracy assumptions, which restrict their validity to weak coupling, small gain/loss contrast, and small detuning. In this work, a non-perturbative formulation of PT symmetric time-delay oscillators is developed based on a delay-difference equation and a scattering matrix representation of the coupling network. The approach treats propagation delay explicitly and does not rely on modal truncation, remaining valid for arbitrary coupling strength, gain/loss imbalance, and resonance detuning. The exact eigenvalue structure of the system is obtained in closed form, yielding a complete characterization of the unbroken and broken PT symmetric regimes as well as the associated exceptional points. A dimensionless order parameter is introduced that governs the symmetry transition over the full parameter space. It is further shown that conventional coupled-mode theory is recovered as an asymptotic limit of the exact formulation for small parameters. The results provide a unified and physically transparent framework for analysing PT symmetric delay systems beyond the weak-coupling limit, with direct implications for the design and optimisation of low-noise oscillators and photonic systems.
tldr: This paper develops a non-perturbative scattering matrix formulation for PT-symmetric time-delay oscillators, providing exact eigenvalue solutions beyond weak coupling.
motivation: Existing coupled-mode theories for PT-symmetric oscillators are limited to weak coupling and small detuning; a more general framework is needed for practical low-noise oscillator design.
method: The authors model the system using a delay-difference equation and a scattering matrix representation of the coupling network, avoiding modal truncation and treating propagation delay explicitly.
result: Closed-form exact eigenvalues are obtained, characterizing unbroken/broken PT symmetry and exceptional points, with a dimensionless order parameter governing the transition.
conclusion: The formulation unifies and extends previous models, offering a physically transparent framework for designing low-noise photonic oscillators.

title: The Schr\"{o}dinger Equation In The Complex Plane And Quantum Entanglement
authors: Vassiliy Lubchenko
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate a continuity equation for the Schr\"odinger equation in the complex space. We define a complex momentum by normalizing the complex current by the particle density. This momentum is a quantum analog of the classical, kinematic momentum analytically continued into the complex plane. The kinematic momentum and the gradient of the wavefunction's phase each represent a fluid-like flow in the complex plane; the phase-gradient flow is incompressible. The zeros of the wavefunction give rise to simple poles in the momentum. The poles manifest as irrotational vortexes in the phase-gradient flow, while critical points of the wavefunction present as rigid body-like rotational flows of the kinematic momentum. A discrete nature of elementary excitations comes about inherently because the quantity of the poles is automatically integer. An exact quantization condition is subsequently formulated, which reduces to the Bohr-Sommerfeld condition in the semiclassical limit. We establish a priori that the Bohr-Sommerfeld condition must be exact for the Harmonic Oscillator. We show that the kinetic energy is a sum of contributions of the average value and fluctuations, respectively, of the kinematic momentum. The zero-point vibrations within bound states are solely due to the fluctuations of the momentum and manifest as rigid-body flows at infinity. The momentum poles -- and hence the wavefunction's zeros -- can be viewed as emergent, consistent with the remarkable property of quantum entanglement exhibited by standing wave solutions of the Schr\"odinger equation.
tldr: The paper reformulates the Schrödinger equation in the complex plane, linking wavefunction zeros to momentum poles and quantum entanglement.
motivation: To understand the geometric and topological structure underlying quantum mechanics, particularly the role of wavefunction zeros and their connection to entanglement.
method: Derives a continuity equation in complex space, defines a complex momentum, and analyzes the flow patterns of kinematic momentum and phase gradient, identifying poles and vortices.
result: Shows that zeros of the wavefunction correspond to simple poles in the momentum, leading to an exact quantization condition and a decomposition of kinetic energy into average and fluctuation parts.
conclusion: The formalism suggests that wavefunction zeros are emergent and underlie quantum entanglement in standing wave solutions, but the connection to standard entanglement theory is not developed.

title: Phase Time Crystals And Pairing In Binary Active Chiral Systems
authors: C. J. O. Reichhardt C. Reichhardt
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a class of dynamic systems we call phase time crystals consisting of a binary assembly of particles with intermediate or long-range repulsive interactions that are subjected to a circular drive of uniform chirality in which each particle species is out of phase from the other by 180 degrees. As a function of the particle density and orbit radius, this system can organize into a rich variety of dynamical crystalline states, including one in which the out of phase particles form bound pairs that assemble into a triangular lattice. We also find stripe phases, overlapping packed crystals, disordered or phase glass states with no diffusion, mixed fluids, and different types of phase-separated states. We show that these states are robust against the addition of thermal fluctuations, and that the paired crystal can melt into a paired fluid. If the drive on each particle species is of opposite chirality, the system forms stripes and packed lattices, but no paired crystal is present. We demonstrate that by modifying the nature of the chiral driving, it is possible to realize numerous kinds of active molecular lattices, including dynamic square spin ice geometries and higher-order complex structures.
tldr: This paper studies dynamical crystalline phases in binary active chiral particle systems, introducing the concept of phase time crystals.
motivation: To explore novel self-organized states in driven non-equilibrium systems with chiral interactions.
method: Numerical simulations of binary particles with repulsive interactions under circular driving with phase offsets.
result: Discovery of paired crystal, stripe, phase glass, and other phases; robustness to thermal fluctuations.
conclusion: Active chiral systems can host a variety of dynamic crystalline phases, including paired structures analogous to molecular lattices.

title: A Qubo Formulation For Nowhere-Zero $k$-Flows
authors: Ali Lotfi, Adam Carter, Mohammad Meysami, Thuan Ha, Kwabena Abrefa Nketia, Steven J. Shirtliffe, Steven Rayan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the encoding of graph problems as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems, which are solvable by either quantum or classical annealers. Yet, the class of problems encoded as QUBO problems has not previously included nowhere-zero flows. Nowhere-zero flows are related to Tutte's [MATH]-flow conjecture and appear in many contexts in graph theory. We provide an encoding of nowhere-zero flows as a QUBO Hamiltonian and prove the correctness of the construction. Our construction yields a Hamiltonian [MATH] whose ground state has zero energy if and only if the graph [MATH] has a nowhere-zero [MATH]-flow. By Tutte's equivalence theorem, zero ground energy is equivalent to [MATH], and the zero-energy degeneracy is given by the flow polynomial [MATH]. In particular, when the ground-state energy is zero, this is also the ground-state degeneracy. The construction uses one-hot variables to represent the edge flow residues modulo [MATH] and auxiliary variables to represent the per-vertex modular quotient. We prove that the correctness of the construction is independent of the choice of orientation, root vertex, and positive penalty weights. We verify the construction on [MATH] examples of graphs and values of [MATH] that include both yes-instances and no-instances. We exhaustively sweep orientations and root choices on selected robustness instances and test a finite suite of positive penalty weights. The resulting Hamiltonian is implemented using the dimod.BinaryQuadraticModel class, which is compatible with the D-Wave Ocean SDK. Quantum-hardware runs and claims about potential speedup using these devices are left to follow-up work.
tldr: This paper presents a QUBO formulation for the nowhere-zero k-flow problem in graph theory, enabling encoding as an optimization problem solvable by quantum or classical annealers.
motivation: Nowhere-zero flows are important in graph theory and related to Tutte's flow conjecture, but have not previously been encoded as QUBO problems. The authors aim to bridge this gap to leverage quantum annealing for graph problems.
method: The authors construct a QUBO Hamiltonian using one-hot variables for edge flow residues modulo k and auxiliary variables for per-vertex modular quotients, proving correctness independent of orientation, root vertex, and penalty weights.
result: The ground state has zero energy if and only if the graph has a nowhere-zero k-flow, with degeneracy given by the flow polynomial. The construction is verified on several graph examples.
conclusion: The QUBO formulation is correct and can be implemented using the D-Wave Ocean SDK, but quantum hardware runs and speedup claims are left for future work.

title: Quantum Counterparty Credit Risk: A Study Of Path-Dependent Derivatives
authors: Sandeep Jha, Richard Oentaryo, Sanjay Sekaran, Vadym Kullish, Rajanikanth Annam, Paul Griffin, Hanan Rosemarin, Nadav Yoran, Nati Erez, Rei Sato
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating potential future exposure (PFE) for path-dependent derivatives, such as FX Target Redemption Forwards (TARFs), represents a formidable computational challenge due to the demand of nested Monte Carlo simulations. We present a hybrid quantum-classical framework that leverages Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) to address this via a reduced-order counterparty credit risk model. Our methodology maps the non-linear TARF payoff -- including cumulative gains and knock-out features -- into a quantum circuit via a two-step formulation, whereby a first-step percentile is computed classically and then used to condition quantum evaluation of subsequent exposure. We employ discretisation of the FX process and a linearised additive approximation of dynamics to enable implementation on current quantum platforms. Developed via the Classiq platform and validated on NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Amazon Braket SV1, our approach achieves relative errors of 1%-8% against classical benchmarks at the 97.5% and 99% confidence levels. While discretisation constraints and approximate monotonicity assumption may introduce bias and limit recovery of the full exposure distribution, our framework offers a tractable testbed for quantum acceleration. Scaling analysis suggests that [MATH]300 logical qubits could enable full 52-week exposure estimation, reducing sample complexity for tail-risk estimation via amplitude estimation at the cost of increased circuit depth.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical framework for estimating potential future exposure of path-dependent derivatives using iterative quantum amplitude estimation.
motivation: Estimating potential future exposure for path-dependent derivatives like FX TARFs is computationally intensive due to nested Monte Carlo simulations; quantum computing may offer acceleration.
method: Maps the TARF payoff into a quantum circuit via a two-step formulation: classical computation of a first-step percentile conditions quantum evaluation of subsequent exposure, using IQAE on a discretized FX process with linearized additive approximation.
result: Achieves relative errors of 1%-8% against classical benchmarks at 97.5% and 99% confidence levels, with scaling analysis suggesting 300 logical qubits could enable full 52-week exposure estimation.
conclusion: The framework provides a tractable testbed for quantum acceleration in credit risk, though discretization constraints and approximate monotonicity may introduce bias.

title: Forward-backward Correspondence Between Stationary Structure And Splitting Probabilities In Active Matter
authors: Derek Frydel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active particles confined by hard walls accumulate at boundaries and may become dynamically adsorbed due to directional persistence. In this work, we show that the same persistence mechanism also gives rise to a finite wall splitting probability, meaning that a particle initialized at a wall can reach the opposite boundary before returning to its starting point. By comparing forward and backward evolution equations directly in position--velocity phase space, we derive exact relations linking stationary distributions and splitting probabilities for run-and-tumble, active Brownian, and active Ornstein--Uhlenbeck particles. In particular, we show that the stationary density is generated by the spatial derivative of the splitting probability, while the distribution of dynamically adsorbed particles at the walls is encoded in wall splitting probabilities. The correspondence is valid in arbitrary spatial dimension and establishes an exact bridge between stationary and first-passage descriptions of confined active matter, revealing them as complementary representations of the same persistence-driven dynamics.
tldr: This paper derives exact relations between stationary distributions and splitting probabilities for active matter particles confined by hard walls.
motivation: To understand how directional persistence in active particles leads to wall accumulation and first-passage properties.
method: Comparing forward and backward evolution equations in position-velocity phase space for run-and-tumble, active Brownian, and active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles.
result: The stationary density is the spatial derivative of the splitting probability, and wall splitting probabilities encode the distribution of dynamically adsorbed particles.
conclusion: Stationary and first-passage descriptions of confined active matter are complementary representations of persistence-driven dynamics.

title: Reflection And Refraction At Nonlinear Temporal Boundaries In Synthetic Lattices
authors: Chong-Xiao Chen, Zheng-Wei Zhou, Xi-Wang Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal boundaries in time-modulated media provide a powerful route toward wave manipulation beyond conventional spatial boundaries. Here, we investigate nonlinear temporal boundaries generated by interaction quenches in a synthetic lattice with exactly solvable interacting dynamics. Unlike conventional temporal boundaries arising from abrupt changes of single-particle dispersion, the present system realizes a self-induced temporal medium in which the propagating wave packet dynamically determines its own effective dispersion and transport properties. By solving the nonlinear Schr\"odinger dynamics analytically, we show that the interaction generates an emergent wave-packet-dependent band structure and a state-dependent temporal refractive response while preserving fully controllable evolution. Based on this framework, we establish a nonlinear temporal-scattering picture and uncover phenomena including amplitude-dependent temporal reflection/refraction and nonlinear temporal birefringence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gradient-induced Bloch oscillations suppress wave-packet diffusion and enable coherent periodic transport with exact state reconstruction. Our results extend temporal reflection and refraction from dispersion-quenched linear systems to interaction-quenched nonlinear media and provide a tractable framework for nonlinear wave manipulation in synthetic lattices.
tldr: This paper studies nonlinear temporal boundaries in synthetic lattices, focusing on wave-packet dynamics and temporal scattering induced by interaction quenches.
motivation: To extend the concept of temporal boundaries from linear dispersion-quenched systems to nonlinear interaction-quenched media, enabling new wave manipulation capabilities.
